t: who does not acknowledge them. Who does not believe that the Creator commanded them (Rashi, Chullin 132b).
has no share in the priesthood. The laws of the priesthood do not apply to him.

a gift that has holiness among them. A gift among these gifts that is forbidden to non-priests and that the priests are commanded to eat (such as terumah), excluding non-sacred gifts, which a priest may give to an Israelite.
inside the wall of the courtyard. Within the sanctified area of the Temple Mount, which includes the Israelites' Courtyard, the Priests' Courtyard, and the structure of the Temple.
and one gift is acquired from the Temple. The place of its acquisition is in the Temple (see below, halacha 8).

and the meat of the guilt offering, whether suspended or definite. A guilt offering that comes for certain transgressions is called a definite guilt offering (Hilchot Shegagot 9:1), whereas a person who is uncertain whether he transgressed a prohibition for which a sin offering is owed brings a suspended guilt offering (ibid. 8:1).
and the communal peace offerings. The two lambs that the community brings as a peace offering on Shavuot (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 1:4).

and the remainder of the omer. The meal offering that the community brings on the sixteenth of Nisan, of which a handful is burned on the altar and the rest is eaten by the priests (Hilchot Temidin u-Musafin 7:12).

and the remainders of the meal offerings of Israelites. Individual meal offerings of an Israelite, of which a handful is burned and the rest is eaten by the priests (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 12:9; but individual meal offerings of a priest are burned entirely on the altar, ibid.).
and the two loaves. The meal offering that the community brings on Shavuot, which is eaten entirely by the priests (Hilchot Temidin u-Musafin 8:11).
and the log of oil of the leper. Which the leper brings upon completing his purification; what remains of the oil after the sprinklings is eaten by the priests (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).

and the portion raised from the thanksgiving offering. The thanksgiving offering is an individual peace offering that comes with bread; the portion raised from it is the breast and thigh of the animal (as in a peace offering), and in addition one loaf from each of the kinds of bread brought with the thanksgiving offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 9:12).
and the portion raised from the nazirite's ram. The breast and thigh of the ram and one loaf from each of the two kinds of bread that come with it, plus the cooked foreleg of the ram (ibid.).
and the first of the shearing. A certain portion of the wool that is given to the priest when a person shears his flock (as detailed below, chapter 10).

and a field of possession. When a person consecrated his ancestral inheritance and another person redeemed it from the Temple treasury, in the Jubilee year it is given to the priests (Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 4:20).

these apply by Torah law only in the Land of Israel. For outside the Land of Israel there is no Torah obligation to separate terumot and challah and to give the first of the shearing, and likewise the law of a field of possession does not apply to fields outside the Land of Israel (see Hilchot Terumot 1:1, below 5:5, below 10:1, Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 8:11).
and terumot and challot of the Land of Israel are eaten only in the Land of Israel. See Hilchot Terumot 2:17.
the gifts. The foreleg, the cheeks, and the maw of a slaughtered animal (below 9:1).
and the firstborn donkey. A donkey that is firstborn to its mother, which is redeemed with a lamb given to the priest (below 12:1-2).
and the robbery of a convert. A convert who was robbed and died without heirs; the robber pays the priests (Hilchot Gezelah 8:4-6).

and the devoted things. A person who said of some of his property 'this is devoted' and did not specify that he meant it for Heaven or for Temple maintenance; it is given to the priests (Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 6:1).
and the gift that is acquired from the Temple etc.. This is the only gift whose place of acquisition is in the Temple, but it is permitted to take it out anywhere (Radbaz).
and the same law applies to the other hides of most holy offerings, all to the priests. But the hides of lesser holy offerings belong to the owners of the offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 5:19).
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:3 and elsewhere.

for they belong to the men of the mishmar. The portions of the offerings given to the priests were divided among the priests serving in the Temple that week (see Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:14), and likewise the first fruits (below 3:1).

and the firstborn etc.. Although a firstborn is given to any priest and not specifically to the men of the mishmar (Hilchot Bechorot 1:15), it must be given only to a male priest, since the priest who receives it must offer it.

as will be explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 5:20 (hides of holy offerings), Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 4:24 (field of possession), ibid. 6:5 (devoted things), Hilchot Gezelah 8:5 (robbery of a convert).

the Sages counted these gifts in a different way. The enumeration and classification of the gifts was done by the Sages differently, as detailed shortly (see Tosefta Challah 2:7-9, Babylonian Talmud Chullin 133b and elsewhere; and see Sifrei Korach section 119, where the gifts are classified in yet another way, but the enumeration of the gifts is similar to Rambam's enumeration here).

four in Jerusalem... and the hides of holy offerings. For the hides are given to the men of the mishmar, whose main place is in Jerusalem (but there is no prohibition to use the hides outside Jerusalem; see Da'at Aharon).

he counted everything raised from lesser holy offerings as one gift etc.. The details of these gifts were mentioned above, halacha 5, in the explanation. According to the Sages' way of counting, all of these are counted as one gift.
and the three of them. An ordinary peace offering, a thanksgiving offering, and a nazirite's ram.
each and every one of them will be explained in its place in the laws of the offerings. In Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot and in other places in the books on Temple service and offerings.
by their words. By enactment of the Sages.

from the cities of Sihon and Og. Cities in the eastern Transjordan that Moses our teacher conquered; there is no Torah obligation of first fruits in them because they are not included in the land flowing with milk and honey (Rivash).
and from Syria. Lands that King David conquered, and their law is like the Land of Israel for certain laws (Hilchot Terumot 1:3-4).
that they are obligated in terumah and tithes by rabbinic law. As explained in Hilchot Terumot 1:1.
mentioned in praise of the land. In the description of the praise of the Land of Israel (Deuteronomy 8:8).
and sukhot figs. A kind of fig that is not pleasant to the palate (Arukh, entry 'sach' 13).
and dusty grapes. That dust was sprinkled on them so that they will not rot (Rabbi Y. Kafih).
and smoked. That do not ripen naturally until smoke is raised beneath them (ibid.).

they have not been sanctified. For it says of first fruits 'you shall take of the first of all the fruit of the ground' (Deuteronomy 26:2), and the Sages learned that only the choicest should be brought (Babylonian Talmud Menachot 84b).

as it says: the fruit of the ground. And a beverage is not a fruit, except for wine and oil, which have special importance, and it is the way to grow olives and grapes for the beverages that come from them.
dried figs. Dried figs.
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.

rather he should leave them there until Atzeret comes and recite over them. He should leave the first fruits in the Temple courtyard until Shavuot, and then he may recite over them the passage of the first fruits declaration (as below 3:10).
not from the new on the old etc.. This Mishnah refers to the previous year, as with terumah (Hilchot Terumot 5:11).
from fruits that formed before the fifteenth of Shevat. That began to ripen before this date, which is the new year for trees (ibid., Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:2).
both planted and growing on their own. A tree that was planted and a tree that grew by itself have the same law.
in their land. In the plural, so even if the land belongs to partners, they are obligated in first fruits.

for it says 'in their land'. Although generally a perforated flowerpot is treated as ground (Hilchot Kil'ayim 1:2, Hilchot Terumot 5:15), for first fruits the Sages learned from the word 'in their land' that one brings only from what grows in the actual ground.
but he brings from what grows on a roof and in a ruin. For the fruits there are considered as growing in the ground.
and layered. Bent a branch of it and buried it in the ground so that another tree would grow from it.
a private path. A path that belongs to another person.
until all that grows is from your soil. That the tree draws only from ground in your possession; in all the cases in this halacha there is some drawing from other ground.
temporarily. For a certain time.
at his fellow's border. At the boundary of his fellow's field.
even though he must keep away. See Hilchot Shekhenim 10:8.

for on this condition Joshua apportioned the land. Joshua divided the land on the condition that people would not be particular with one another in these cases regarding the mitzvah of first fruits (and in Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:3 Rambam detailed Joshua's conditions concerning monetary matters between a person and his fellow, and did not write there the condition mentioned here, which is between a person and God; Me'ir Arukh, Arukh ha-Shulchan 139:5).
sharecroppers and tenant farmers. Those who work a field for a certain percentage of the yield or a fixed amount of the yield.
and buy their lands from them at a discount. They force the landowner to sell it at a low price.
and even if the owners gave up hope. For in land there is no giving up hope and it never passes into the possession of the robber (Hilchot Gezelah 8:14).
one who buys one tree... and one who buys three trees. The law of one who buys two trees will be explained below 4:4.
and one who buys three trees has land. For this is the law in the laws of sale, that the buyer receives the ground between the trees (Hilchot Mechirah 24:1-2).

and although he has only the trees alone etc.. Although in the laws of sale, buying three trees gives the buyer the ground only when certain conditions are met (see ibid. halachot 1-4), for first fruits these conditions are not needed, since the trees themselves are considered land, because they occupy a large area of root-drawing (see Kesef Mishneh, Or Sameach, and Chiddushei Rabbi Chaim).
one who buys detached fruits and bought the ground. A person who bought detached fruits and afterward bought the ground in which they grew.
as we have explained. Hilchot Terumot 1:10.

an asherah that was nullified. A tree planted for idol worship and forbidden to benefit from (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:3), which was afterward nullified from being an idol in a way that makes it permitted to benefit from (ibid. 8:8).

for first fruits are like Temple offerings. For one may not bring to the Temple something repulsive, even when there is no prohibition against benefiting from it (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 4:7-8).
and added to them. Additional fruits of the same kind.

that he adorned them. Decorated them by adding fruits of another kind (Mishnah Bikkurim 3:10, and see the Commentary to the Mishnah and Chiddushei Maharich there) from the seven species (as below at the end of the halacha).
that ripened first. That ripened earliest (even if it has not yet ripened fully, as below).
with reed. A plant used in their time for tying, and likewise any other marking (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:1).

he separates from the pure for the impure at the outset. He separates from other pure fruits for the fruits that became impure (unlike terumah, where one should not separate from the pure for the impure at the outset, Hilchot Terumot 5:7).

it seems to me that he does not separate for the impure, since one does not separate to waste. And here the first fruits would go to waste since they cannot be used once they became impure, as he goes on to explain (see Da'at Aharon and Or Sameach; for the principle mentioned here see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:9, Hilchot Me'ilah 4:7).

he does not heat the oven with them as with impure terumah, since they are like Temple offerings. Terumah that became impure is burned, and the priest is permitted to benefit from its burning (Hilchot Terumot 2:14). And first fruits that became impure must also be burned (ibid. 15:21), but one does not benefit from the burning, like holy offerings that became impure (see Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 19:1).
and rotted. Decayed.
were plundered. Were robbed.
he should not send them with a messenger. Since the messenger cannot recite the first fruits declaration, as below 4:2.
to a minor at the outset in order to send them with a messenger, it is permitted to send them. Since they were not obligated in the recitation (Da'at Aharon).
and we have already explained. Hilchot Terumot 15:20.
after they entered etc.. After they entered, even if afterward they left.
to the men of the mishmar. To the priests serving in the Temple that week.
as we have explained in the laws of terumah. 15:20.
the declaration. The first fruits declaration, as below, halacha 10.
and first fruits that went out... are permitted to be eaten. Unlike the meat of offerings, which becomes disqualified by going out (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 11:6).
eating first fruits is like eating terumah for every purpose. As explained in Hilchot Terumot chapters 6-7 who may eat terumah, and in chapter 11, halachot 1-15, the manner of eating terumah.
to a mourner before burial. A person mourning one of his relatives on the day of death (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:6).
bringing to the place. To the Temple, and they must be eaten in Jerusalem.
just as a pure Israelite is flogged etc.. Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:1.
unlike terumah. The reason is explained in Hilchot Terumot 7:3.
disciplinary lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
and wheat on top of them. For wheat is more important than barley.

and olives on top of them etc.. For tree fruits are more important than ground fruits, and among the tree fruits themselves he puts the soft ones above the hard ones so that the soft ones are not crushed, and therefore figs are on top of everything (Da'at Aharon).
palm leaves. Palm fronds.
and reed-grass. A plant used for making mats and baskets.

clusters of grapes on the outside. For the beauty of the mitzvah, and although the grapes are not in the inner space of the vessel, they are considered placed in the vessel since he carries them by means of the vessel (Da'at Aharon).
and the vessel returns to its owner. Since it has importance of its own and is not subordinate to the first fruits.
and if the first fruits became impure, the baskets do not go to the priests. Since the priest does not receive impure first fruits (as below 4:10), he also does not receive the basket.
from the sides of the baskets. And not on top of them, so that they do not soil the fruits (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:5).

they are offered as burnt offerings. As a burnt offering, since they were accustomed to consecrate them together with the first fruits. But the young pigeons they held they brought as a gift to the priests (Radbaz).
to make the declaration over the first fruits. To tell what happened and to give thanks to the Lord (see Tosefta ki-Fshutah Bikkurim p. 850 and the note there).
they make him recite it. They read before him and he repeats word for word.
the court instituted etc.. Since at the beginning of the Second Temple period many did not know the holy language (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:7).
he himself. For it says 'and the priest shall take the basket from your hand' (Deuteronomy 26:4; Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:4).

and holds it by its rims, and the priest places his hand beneath it and waves. The owner of the fruits holds the rim of the basket at its upper edge, and the priest places his hand underneath the basket, and so the waving of the first fruits is performed.
and prostrates himself. By stretching out hands and feet toward the Sanctuary (Tiferet Yisrael Bikkurim 3:6, Da'at Aharon).

'and the priest shall take the basket from your hand'. And the Sages learned by analogy from the peace offering, which the Torah specifies requires waving, where the term 'hand' is used (Leviticus 7:30; Babylonian Talmud Sukkah 47b).

and the tumtum. A person whose reproductive organs are covered, so that it is not possible to know whether he is male or female (Hilchot Ishut 2:25). [Note: in the Commentary to the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes this word 'tumtum'.]
and the androginos. A person who has both male and female reproductive organs (ibid. halacha 24).

and they cannot say 'which You, Lord, have given me'. For in the first fruits declaration a person gives thanks for his portion in the Land of Israel, and therefore it is said only if the one bringing the first fruits has a portion in the land, and the Land of Israel was divided only among males (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 1:5).
guardians. Those appointed over the property of orphans.
and the slave. A Canaanite slave.
who cannot say 'which You have given me'. For only one to whom the land from which the first fruits are brought belongs can recite the first fruits declaration.

and Abraham was first given the oath that his children would inherit the land. For this reason a convert can say in the blessing for the land in Birkat ha-Mazon 'that You gave as an inheritance to our fathers,' since the land was promised to Abraham and his descendants and converts are considered children of Abraham (Responsa of Rambam 96; and compare the law stated regarding the tithe confession in Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni ve-Neta Revai 11:17, and see the explanation there).
cities of pasture-land. The forty-eight cities, around each of which there is a surrounding area called a migrash (Hilchot Shemitah ve-Yovel 13:1-2).

for it is doubtful whether he has land. The Sages were uncertain whether in this case the land passes into the buyer's possession together with the trees, and in monetary law the rule is that the burden of proof is on the one seeking to take from his fellow, and therefore the land remains in the seller's possession (Hilchot Mechirah 24:6), but regarding first fruits, a Torah doubt is treated stringently and therefore he must bring them, but he does not recite the declaration, since the declaration applies only to definite first fruits (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 1:6).
for Temple maintenance. For the property of the Temple.
and one does not bring non-sacred food into the courtyard. It is forbidden to bring non-sacred food into the Temple courtyard (Hilchot Sheḥitah 2:3).
and he separates terumah and tithes from them since they are doubtfully non-sacred. But definite first fruits are exempt from terumot and tithes.

for whatever is unfit for recitation because of doubt, the recitation is indispensable for it. Since the owner of the first fruits is in principle obligated in the recitation and is unable to recite only because of the doubt, the recitation is indispensable. But the messenger is unfit for the recitation because he is not obligated in it, and therefore the recitation is not indispensable when he brings by means of a messenger.

and if he separated, he brings and does not recite. The buyer may bring them just as one is permitted to make the whole field first fruits (above 2:17), but the recitation applies only to first fruits he is obligated in.
one who sells his field for the fruits. In a way that the buyer has the right to eat the fruits but has no right in the land itself (for example, to build on it).

for acquisition of the fruits is not like acquisition of the body. And the buyer cannot say 'which You have given me,' but he must bring first fruits since the obligation cannot be removed from the field (Arukh ha-Shulchan 141:8).

but a person brings first fruits from his wife's property and recites etc.. For regarding his wife's property there is a special extension from the word 'and your house,' that his wife is like his own body and he may say of her property 'which You have given me' (ibid. 141:7).

even if his wife died etc.. Although at the time of taking the first fruits to bring them up to Jerusalem he is like a messenger (for the land belongs to his wife), and at the time of bringing them to the priest he is the owner (for he inherited his wife), and apparently there is no 'taking and bringing as one' (see below, halacha 8), nevertheless since his wife is like his own body, it is as though the land were his from the start.
at a time when the Jubilee is observed. At a time when the laws of the Jubilee apply, and then lands return to their owners when the Jubilee year arrives.

he brings and recites etc.. The buyer brings and recites in all the years the land is in his possession until it returns to the seller in the Jubilee, since at the time of sale the seller is not sure whether the land will return to him, and from his perspective the sale is absolute.

but if it returned etc.. If the seller sold the land again after it returned to him in the Jubilee, the buyer does not recite the first fruits declaration, since now the seller is confident that the land will return to him and that the buyer receives only the right to eat the fruits until the next Jubilee.
in danger. In mortal danger.
he brings and does not recite. For as long as he has not actually inherited from him, the land is not his, and he has the law of a messenger.
and the messenger died on the way etc.. And likewise if the owner decided for another reason to bring them himself (Da'at Aharon).
until the taking and bringing are as one. The first fruits declaration depends on the taking and the bringing being done by one person.

one is not liable for a fifth on them as for first fruits. A non-priest who ate terumah or first fruits unintentionally must pay their value plus a fifth (Hilchot Terumot 10:1, 10:4). However, if he ate first fruits that were separated as a replacement for first fruits that were lost, he need not add a fifth, since the obligation of a fifth applies only to the first (Arukh ha-Shulchan 141:12).
he scatters. Throws away, since the priest cannot use them, but burns them without benefiting from it (as above 2:19).
and the spring dried up. That watered the field.
or the tree was cut down. From which he brought the first fruits.
and until Chanukah. And after Chanukah they do not bring at all (above 2:6).

but only at the time of rejoicing, from the festival of Shavuot until the end of the festival of Sukkot. For from Shavuot to Sukkot they harvest the crop and bring it into the house (Rashi, Deuteronomy 26:11), and the festival of Sukkot itself is 'the time of our rejoicing.'
and the principal and the fifth. Which a non-priest who ate unintentionally pays (see above, halacha 9, in the explanation).
and the gifts of an animal. The foreleg, the cheeks, and the maw (as explained below 9:1).
he may buy slaves with them etc.. The priest is not obligated to eat these gifts, but he may sell them and buy with them even things that are not eaten.
they are neutralized at one in a hundred and one. They are nullified in a mixture of non-sacred produce when the ratio in the mixture is one to a hundred of non-sacred.
like terumah. Hilchot Terumot 13:1 (and ibid. 15:21 it is stated that this is the law also for first fruits).

they forbid in any amount when mixed with their own kind. When they are mixed with fruits of the same kind, the first fruits are not neutralized at all, and the entire mixture is forbidden to non-priests and must be eaten according to the laws of first fruits.
like second tithe. For when it is mixed with other fruits, the entire mixture must be eaten in purity according to the law of second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 6:14).

they made them like something that has a permitting factor. It is a rule that when something that has a way of being permitted in a certain manner (such as new grain, which becomes permitted after the omer is offered) is mixed with another thing of its kind, it is not neutralized even at one in several thousand (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:10; and in halacha 12 there it is explained that in a mixture of one kind with a different kind, something that has a permitting factor is neutralized if it does not impart flavor).

and even though first fruits are forbidden to non-priests even in Jerusalem. Although non-priests have no way to eat first fruits permissibly, the Sages were strict in Jerusalem and forbade the mixture also to non-priests, since priests can eat it there (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 2:2).

even seed of first fruits etc.. Crops of first fruits that were sown outside Jerusalem are permitted, since they also grow from the power of the soil, which is non-sacred (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:14; Ma'aser Sheni ve-Neta Revai 10:21). But when sown in Jerusalem, which is the place for eating them, the Sages were strict about this.

all the towns of the ma'amad gather in the town of the ma'amad. The ma'amad are chosen men who are present at the offering of the communal offerings as representatives of all Israel, and they were divided into twenty-four ma'amadot serving by weekly rotation. During the rotation, the men of the ma'amad who live near Jerusalem enter the Temple, and those who are far gather in a synagogue chosen for that purpose (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 6:1-2). At the time of bringing up the first fruits, all the people living in the towns belonging to that ma'amad gather in the town where the chosen synagogue is.
because of the tent of impurity. Lest there be corpse impurity there, which defiles all who are under the roof above it (Hilchot Tumat Met 1:10).
and the ox goes before them. Some explain that this ox was brought near as the peace offering that comes with the first fruits (as above 3:12; Rivamatz on Bikkurim 3:3, Responsa of Rashba 1:291).
and a crown of olive. A crown made of olive branches.
and the flute plays before them. A person playing a flute walks at the head of the procession.

two hands of the day. Two thirds of the day (for in the middle of the day, in the hot hours, they would rest), so that they would perform the mitzvah with joy and not out of weariness (Chazon David on Tosefta Bikkurim 2:8).

and adorned their first fruits and arranged them. They decorated the first fruits, and gave them a pleasant appearance by displaying the finest fruits on the outside (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:3).
and the governors. The heads of Israel (ibid.).
and the deputies. The heads of the priests (ibid.).
and the treasurers. Those in charge of the Temple's works and its property (ibid.).

all the craftsmen in Jerusalem stand before them. To honor the group bringing the first fruits. And although during their work they are not obligated to stand before Torah scholars (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:2), here they stand out of respect for the public (Commentary to the Mishnah Bikkurim 3:3).

until he leaves some. Until he leaves some of the dough for himself, since challah is called 'the first,' and if nothing remains after it, it is not the first (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 1:9; and see also Hilchot Terumot 3:5).
and by rabbinic law. An enactment of the Sages.

one twenty-fourth of the dough, so that it will be enough to be a gift to the priest. For this percentage of the minimum quantity subject to challah is an amount sufficient to be a gift (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 2:7).
and the baker. The baker.
so as not to divide among the householder's dough. The Sages instituted a uniform amount for all householders.
he separates one forty-eighth. A small amount, because it is destined to be burned and one should minimize impure holy things (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 2:7).
so that a sinner not be rewarded. So that he not profit from having made the dough impure.
for heating. To benefit from its burning (Hilchot Terumot 2:14).
as we have explained regarding terumah. Hilchot Terumot 1:26.
that entered the land. And made dough of them in the land (Radbaz).
are obligated in challah. By Torah law, for we follow the place where the dough was made and not the place where the grain grew.
are exempt. By Torah law, and are obligated by rabbinic law as explained in the following halachot.
and one does not bring challah of outside the Land into the Land, just as one does not bring terumah and first fruits from there. See Hilchot Terumot 2:17, above 2:1.

and if he brought it, he leaves it until Passover eve and it is burned. For the challah cannot be eaten, as it has become impure with the impurity of foreign lands (see the next halacha in the explanation), and it cannot be burned right away lest people think that pure challah is being burned (as the challah did not become impure with an evident impurity known to all), and therefore they wait until Passover eve and burn it with the rest of the chametz (Hilchot Terumot there, Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 4:10).

all the land that the returnees from Babylonia took possession of. The area of the Land of Israel that the exiles who came up from Babylonia took possession of and sanctified with a sanctity that stands forever.

and the rest of the Land of Israel that those who came up from Egypt took possession of etc.. The parts that Israel conquered when they first entered the land and were not taken possession of again by the returnees from Babylonia. The sanctity of those parts lapsed when they were exiled from the land (for an extensive explanation and the detail of the borders of those who came up from Egypt and from Babylonia see Hilchot Terumot 1:5-8).

that the first challah is impure, since that land was not sanctified in the days of Ezra. For the Sages decreed impurity on lands outside the Land of Israel ('impurity of the lands of the nations,' Hilchot Tumat Met chapter 11), including the territory taken possession of by those who came up from Egypt but not by those who came up from Babylonia (Da'at Aharon, and see there that some disagree on this matter, and see Melekhet Shlomo Tumat Met 11:6).
they separate from it challah of one forty-eighth. As for impure dough (above, halacha 4), and with this separation he fulfills the mitzvah of challah.

and separate a second challah etc.. The Sages instituted separating an additional challah, so that people not think that it is permitted to burn pure terumah (including challah), since the law of impurity of the lands of the nations is not known to all.

they separate two challot etc.. Below in halachot 10-11 it is explained that challah of outside the Land is eaten by a priest who is pure from seminal impurity. Our halacha deals with a case where the owner of the dough does not want to look for such a priest, in which case he must burn the challah so that people not say that challah is eaten in impurity, and he separates another challah for eating so that the mitzvah of eating challah is not forgotten, and this challah may be eaten by all priests, even those with a discharge, men and women, since he has already fulfilled his obligation with the first challah.
because of corpse impurity. Since there are no ashes of the red heifer and it is impossible to be purified of corpse impurity, everyone is presumed impure (see Radbaz).
and it has a fundamental name by Torah law. For when all Israel is on it, they are obligated in challah by Torah law.

and from Kezib to Amanah they separate a second for the priest to eat... as it was originally. Although today impurity is known to all and they will not come to say 'we saw pure terumah burned,' nevertheless the law remains as it was originally.
a mature priest. An adult, who may have a seminal emission.

even though he did not wait for nightfall. Although purification is not complete until the day ends after immersion, and the impure may not eat terumah by Torah law until the stars come out (Hilchot Terumot 7:2), in challah, which is rabbinic, they were lenient (see also ibid. halachot 8-9).
who cannot bless. For it is forbidden to bless while exposed (Hilchot Berakhot 1:9).
with her whole face against the ground. That she sits with her lower face (private parts) pressed against the ground and covered.
and similar to her. Impure people from whose bodies impurity issues, as above, halacha 10.
that does not warn about touching it. There is no prohibition against making challah of outside the Land impure, since it is impure anyway.
as we have explained. Above, halachot 10-11.

it is permitted to eat it with a non-priest at one table. Since challah of outside the Land is rabbinic, they did not decree to forbid this out of concern that the non-priest would eat of the challah (like terumah of outside the Land, and unlike terumah of the Land of Israel, where they did decree; Hilchot Terumot 11:7).

that it does not render mixtures forbidden, even if it was mixed in equal parts. If a certain amount of challah of outside the Land was mixed with an equal amount of non-sacred produce, everything is permitted for non-priests to eat, for the Sages were lenient in the laws of challah of outside the Land.
and they give it to a priest who is an am ha-aretz etc.. Unlike terumah and challah by Torah law, which are not given to an am ha-aretz because he is presumed impure (Hilchot Terumot 6:2).

and there is no concern of a priest who assists in his gifts, which is forbidden. It is forbidden for priests to assist in agricultural work in order to receive priestly gifts (ibid. 12:18), and for challah of outside the Land it is permitted.
to eat first and afterward separate the challah. To bake the dough and eat from it on the basis that he will separate challah afterward (see also Hilchot Ma'aser 1:5).
challah is called terumah. As it says: 'Of the first of your dough you shall raise up a cake as a raised offering' (Numbers 15:20).
is taken only from what is adjoining. One may not separate from produce in one place for produce in another place (Hilchot Terumot 3:17).

and is not taken from the pure for the impure at the outset. One should not separate from pure dough for impure dough. After the fact, if he did separate, he has fulfilled the obligation (see also ibid. 5:7).
and everything we said regarding terumah, that it may not be separated etc.. People who may not separate terumah, as detailed in Hilchot Terumot 4:2-14.
and everything we said regarding terumah, that it may not be separated from this for that. Ibid. chapter 5.
and anyone who does not eat terumah. Ibid. chapters 6-9.

for in dough there is no bad and good etc.. Unlike fruits, in which there is bad and good, and therefore a blind person and a drunk, who cannot select the good fruits, do not separate terumah at the outset (Hilchot Terumot 4:4).

one who buys from the baker separates from the fresh etc.. One who buys from a baker who did not separate challah separates from fresh baked goods baked today for baked goods baked yesterday, and even from different kinds of loaves baked in different pans. For separating terumot and tithes, he cannot tithe from one kind for another out of concern that the flour was taken from different people (see Hilchot Ma'aser 14:5 and the explanation there), but in separating challah there is no problem, since the obligation of challah falls on the baker himself at the time he prepares the dough and not on the owners of the flour.
and spelt. Desert wheat (Commentary to the Mishnah Kil'ayim 1:1).
and oats and rye. Kinds of desert barley (ibid.).
and grain that has not reached a third. That has not grown a third of its growth.
even though they are exempt from terumah. Hilchot Terumot 2:9-11.

they are obligated in challah. For the obligation of challah applies only when dough is made (below 8:4), and the one who makes dough owns it, even if he acquired the wheat from ownerless property or from gifts to the poor. And one who makes dough from grain that has not reached the stage of growth that obligates in terumah (reaching a third) becomes obligated in challah at the time of making the dough, because dough made from such grain can become leavened, and any dough that comes to leavening is obligated in challah (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 1:3).

first tithe that was taken early in the ears of grain, from which its terumah was taken. That the Levite preceded the priest and received tithe from the ears before the great terumah was separated from them, and separated from them terumat ma'aser.

even though it contains a portion of great terumah. Although this tithe contains a certain percentage that was supposed to be great terumah, the obligation to separate great terumah was removed from it (Hilchot Terumot 3:13), but the obligation of challah that applies at the time the dough is made was not removed (Da'at Aharon).

and the remainder of the omer, the two loaves, and the showbread, when all those gifts are redeemed. These meal offerings are made from a certain amount of well-sifted flour, and any excess over the required amount is redeemed and eaten by anyone (Hilchot Temidin u-Musafin 7:12, 8:3-4). While they are sacred they are exempt from challah, but since they were redeemed and went out to non-sacred status before the dough was made, they are obligated in challah (see below 8:6).
dough of second tithe in Jerusalem. Which it is a mitzvah to eat there in purity.
and dough of the Sabbatical year. That was made from wheat that has the sanctity of the Sabbatical year.

and doubtfully mixed with terumah. 'Mixed with terumah' (medumma) is a mixture of terumah and non-sacred produce in which the terumah was not neutralized and the entire mixture is forbidden to non-priests (see Hilchot Terumot 13:2), and 'doubtfully mixed' is, for example, where there was a pile of non-sacred flour and next to it a pile of terumah flour, and a little terumah flour fell into one of the piles, in which case the Sages did not forbid the pile of non-sacred flour (see ibid. halacha 14).

are obligated in challah. Although all these doughs have an aspect of sanctity, they are not considered sacred dough, which is exempt from challah, because they are permitted to be eaten by the owner of the dough.
but what is mixed with terumah is exempt from challah. For the entire mixture is treated as terumah, which is exempt from challah (see Rivash).
loaves of the thanksgiving offering. Loaves brought together with a thanksgiving offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 9:17-21).
and the wafers of the nazirite. Which the nazirite brings with his offering (ibid. halacha 23).
since he intends that if it is not sold he will eat it. For he does not consecrate them when he makes them, but leaves for himself the possibility of eating them as non-sacred.
and one who makes dough for many. In order to distribute it to many after baking (and see below, halacha 19, whether he distributes the dough while it is still dough).
one who makes dough from tevel. From flour from which terumot and tithes were not separated (usually terumot and tithes are separated before making grain into flour).

it may not be eaten until he takes challah from it. Until he separates challah from the dough and intends to also exempt the terumah from the obligation of challah, for when a person separates terumah only after making dough from the grain, the terumah too is obligated in challah.
for an animal or a beast it is exempt. For it says 'when you eat of the bread of the land' (Numbers 15:19), which means human eating (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 1:8).
dogs' dough. Dough that shepherds make for dogs, made from flour mixed with bran (wheat refuse) and fit for human food only under pressure.
they inform him that he does not need. So that he not think that his challah is being fed to a non-priest (Shach, Yoreh De'ah, letter yod of subsection 3).
and why were we not concerned etc.. As we were concerned in the separation of terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 4:15).
for if an Israelite wishes etc.. There is a simple way to be exempted from the obligation to separate challah (below, halacha 15).

if it has the taste of grain, it is obligated in challah. Although the amount of rice is greater than the amount of wheat, since the rice follows the wheat and all the dough is fit to leaven (explained according to the Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:1).
the sourdough. Leavened dough used to make other dough rise.
whether in the ground. In a pit in the ground by means of coals.
and the pan. A kind of frying pan.
to cook it in a pot. In a pot with water.
parched grain. Flour made from roasted wheat.
to make it sun-work. Intending to dry it in the sun (or cook it in water).
and completed making it bread. After he prepared the dough, he changed his mind and baked it.
or began to bake it into bread. That at the time of preparing the dough he was already obligated in challah.
and likewise parched grain that he kneaded to bake into bread. That he decided not to eat it with water or honey but to bake it into bread, and baked it.
that is made for kutach. That is baked in order to crumble it and put it into kutach, a food made from whey, bread crumbs, and salt.
made it into loaves. Baked it in the shape of ordinary bread.
like boards. Like planks, in that he was not particular about a nice shape.
a full omer. The quantity of manna that each person received in the wilderness (Exodus 16:16).
two kavs less a fifth. A volume measure of 1.8 kav, since the omer is a tenth of an ephah (ibid. 16:36) and an ephah is 18 kavs.
and the revi'it is two fingers by two fingers etc.. The volume of a revi'it is 2 fingers by 2 fingers with a height of 2.7 fingers.
and all fingers are the width of a thumb of the hand. The measure of a finger is measured by the width of the thumb of the hand.
and the two measures come out as one. The measures correspond to each other.

of the wheat flour of Egypt. The weight measure given here, which corresponds to the volume of 43.2 eggs, is according to wheat flour of Egypt. However, the weight varies between wheat and barley and between kinds of flour, and therefore one should not measure by weight except roughly and in accordance with that kind, whereas the determining measure is by volume (Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 2:6).
to make his dough less than the measure each time. To prepare small doughs one after another, instead of one large dough.
biting into one another. Touching and stuck together in such a way that if they are separated, a little of one will be torn from the other.
a board that has no rim. A surface that has no sides around it.
challah by their words. A case in which the obligation of challah is only by rabbinic law.
that he did not sift. That he did not sift it.
with fine bran. Thin husks.
is obligated in challah. Since sometimes dough is made in this way.
coarse bran. Coarse husks above the fine bran.
is not obligated in challah. For this is not the way of preparing dough.
to make it sourdough to divide it. To sell small leavened portions of dough to customers.

for if it is not sold he will make it into bread. And since he has in mind the possibility that he will bake all the dough together and become obligated in challah, he is obligated (compare above, halacha 5, and see Commentary to the Mishnah Challah 1:7).

but one who makes dough to divide it as dough is exempt. A person who kneaded dough of the quantity obligated in challah and intends to divide it before baking into small pieces that lack the required measure is exempt.
to make sourdough for them. So that each woman will take a little sourdough for baking in her home.
and they bit into one another. Stuck together so that if they are separated, a little of one will be torn from the other.
for ordinarily two people are particular. Generally people are particular that another person's dough not be mixed with theirs.
if they were both. The two biting doughs.
for ordinarily one is not particular etc.. A person who has two doughs of the same kind can be presumed not to be particular if they become mixed.

and how do they combine etc.. Oats and rye are a kind of barley, and spelt is a kind of wheat (Hilchot Berakhot 3:1, and see also below 8:4). But because spelt also resembles the kinds of barley, it combines with them too (see Commentary to the Mishnah and Rash on Kil'ayim 1:1). Therefore, wheat dough combines only with spelt, and spelt dough combines with all the kinds.
new dough does not combine with old. Dough made from this year's grain that bites into dough made from last year's grain do not combine to complete the measure.

so that they not say one may separate from the new for the old. The law of combining doughs that bite into each other depends on their being one kind, and therefore by Torah law new and old dough combine. But the Sages said that they do not combine so that people do not come to permit separating from new dough for old dough or vice versa, since separating from one for the other is forbidden by Torah law (like the law of separating terumah explained in Hilchot Terumot 5:11, and challah was equated to terumah in the laws of its separation, as above 5:14).

and one should not separate from the middle of both etc.. If he combined the doughs, he cannot separate challah from them because of the aforementioned decree of the Sages, even when he separates from each dough for itself, for example by separating from the middle and taking a little from this one and a little from that one. Likewise, he cannot separate between the doughs without separating challah from them, since he became obligated in challah by Torah law when he combined them. Therefore the solution is to bring another dough.

he should bring another dough, new or old, and add it to them to complete the measure. He should complete one of the doughs so that there is a challah measure from grain of one year (new or old), and separate from that dough for all, for when there is a challah measure from grain of one year, there is a distinction, and it is permitted to add to it dough from grain of another year and they are considered one dough (Rivash, and see Radbaz, who explained differently).
when does this apply?. That two kinds, or new and old, do not combine (Rivash).
as we have explained. Above 6:15.
mixed with terumah. For an explanation of the term see above 6:4.

dough of consecrated property. That was consecrated to the Temple after it was made into dough and became obligated in challah, and being sacred it is exempt from challah until it is redeemed (see below 8:6-7).
for the first challot are nothing. For they were separated from exempt doughs, and only after the doughs touched did they become obligated in challah.

for it had no time of obligation when they were gentiles. The dough came to the obligation of challah only after they converted (and had it been fit for the obligation of challah before the conversion, it would have been exempt forever, according to the rule explained in the next halacha).

for it already had a time of obligation etc.. For when the dough had the required measure it was fit to become obligated, but it was exempted from challah because it was made to be divided. And any dough that is exempt at the time it was fit to become obligated is no longer obligated (see also below 8:7-9).

if the dough was between the gentile and the Israelite in partnership. In full partnership for all purposes, without intent to divide (unlike what is spoken of in the previous halachot, where only the making was together with the intention to divide after the making; Kesef Mishneh).
and they divided. Afterward they changed their minds and decided to divide.

the Israelite's is obligated. Since it had no time of obligation before, for the gentile's share in the dough counts for nothing with regard to the Israelite, and it turns out that the Israelite's share was completed to the challah measure only after the Israelite added his own.

and the gentile's is exempt. Like a gentile who had dough of the measure before he converted (which is no longer obligated), for the Israelite's share in the partnership completes the gentile's share to the challah measure.
he brings etc.. In order to correct the sourdough from which challah was not separated.
from what is adjoining. From what is near, as above 5:13.

for tevel in its own kind forbids in any amount. Tevel that was mixed with non-sacred produce of its own kind is not neutralized at any proportion, but the entire mixture is considered tevel, because there is a way to permit it by separating challah (a 'thing that has a permitting factor'; Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:10).
dough that is tevel for challah. That is obligated in challah and has not yet been separated.

for the second does not make a third in non-sacred things. Anything that touches a primary source of impurity becomes 'first-degree impure,' and what touches a first becomes 'second-degree impure,' and so on (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:8). However, a second-degree impure does not make non-sacred things impure as a 'third degree,' since only terumah (including challah) and holy things become impure through a second-degree impure (see Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 11:2-4).
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 11:15.
and it is permitted to cause impurity to non-sacred things in the Land of Israel. See also Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 16:9.

one pure and one impure. For one does not separate from this for that (above 5:13), unless he joins them in the manner explained below (and similar to the law of separating terumah from the pure for the impure, as explained in Hilchot Terumot 5:7).
the challah of both. The challah measure for both doughs.

and draws from the impure to the pure the size of an egg. He joins the impure dough with the pure dough by means of a piece of dough the size of an egg that he took from the pure dough. And although this piece becomes second-degree impure, he need not be concerned, since it is permitted to make non-sacred things impure. And the pure dough, and the challah touching it, remain in their purity, since dough that is tevel for challah has the law of non-sacred and is not made impure by contact with a second-degree impure, as above (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).

to separate on it as he goes etc.. That when he makes another dough he will not separate challah from it, but will designate a certain portion in the first dough for the challah of the second dough, and so dough after dough until the first dough becomes entirely challah.
for the challah of demai. Challah of doubt.
one who separates his challah from flour. Separated challah from the flour before making it into dough, and gave it to a priest.
and robbery in the hand of the priest. For he must return the flour to its owner.
and the rest of the dough. The flour from which challah was separated, which he made into dough.
an omer. The measure of challah (as above 6:15).

he separates the challah from the beginning of what is kneaded... provided that no flour remains in the vessel that has not been mixed with water, of the measure of an omer. He separates from the dough formed by the first quantity of flour that was mixed with water, even though some flour has not yet been mixed, but on the condition that the flour that has not been mixed does not contain the measure that obligates in challah (an 'omer'). [Note: in the Commentary to the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes the word 'when' as 'amatai'.]

for it says 'the first of your dough'. From this the Sages derived that one may separate from the time of the beginning of making the dough (Jerusalem Talmud Challah 3:1). With pure challah it is proper to do so in order to reduce the possibility that the dough will become impure before challah is separated (Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 3:3; however, with impure challah it is preferable to separate at the end of making the dough when it has all become one body, since then the main obligation applies, as below, halacha 4; commentators of Rambam, and so it emerges from the Jerusalem Talmud there).

and if he said: this is challah for the dough, the sourdough, and the flour that remains etc.. If he separated challah at the start of making the dough and stipulated that sanctity not take effect on it until the dough is completed, it is permitted to do so even if at the time of separation flour of the measure of an omer remained unmixed.
there is nothing in it. It is permitted to do so.
as we have explained. Above 6:16.

once it is rolled in wheat... or kneaded in barley. The process of making dough begins with pouring water into a bowl containing the flour and mixing the water and flour. In the first stage a kind of dough crumbs forms, and these crumbs are kneaded again until a uniform, pliable dough is obtained that can be shaped and worked; this is the 'rolling.' This process is done with wheat flour, which has much gluten (a sticky protein) that causes the dough to hold together. By contrast, with barley flour, whose gluten content is relatively low, the dough does not stick together well but tends to crumble and cannot be kneaded, and therefore the preparation of the dough is completed by 'sealing,' that is, joining the parts of the dough into a solid lump without holes.
liable to death. At the hands of Heaven, like one who eats before separating terumah (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:19).
one who eats of it is flogged like anyone who eats tevel. And like anyone who transgresses a prohibition for which one is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1).
disciplinary lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
that was mixed with terumah. Into which terumah or challah fell.
exempt. As above 6:4.
and once it is rolled, it is obligated. If it was mixed with terumah after rolling, it had already become obligated in challah at the time of rolling, and the mixing does not remove this obligation.
and redeemed it. From the Temple treasury.
or acquired it. From ownerless property.

and a non-priest who ate etc.. A person who is not a priest ('a stranger') who unintentionally ate terumah must pay its value plus a fifth (see Hilchot Terumot 10:1), and likewise if he unintentionally ate challah (ibid. halacha 4). However, if he took doubtful challah from a priest and ate it, he must pay him only its value without the addition, for a priest who wishes to collect the addition from him as well must bring proof that it is indeed challah.
for which a doubt of impurity arose. For which there is a doubt whether it became impure.
and her challah is burned. Like impure challah (above 5:4).

a doubtful impurity whose definite case would make non-sacred things impure by Torah law. If a doubt of impurity arose in dough, of a kind of impurity that if it were certain would also make non-sacred dough impure.

since they became tevel for challah. Since this non-sacred dough became obligated in challah from the time of rolling while it was still pure, they were strict about it like challah itself, which it is forbidden to make impure.
it is left hanging, neither eaten nor burned. It is left until it becomes impure or rots, for it may not be eaten lest it be impure and may not be burned lest it be pure.
a person should not at the outset make his dough in impurity. And nowadays dough is made in impurity and challah is separated from it (above 5:9).
the water. That is fit for immersion.
miles. A mil is a distance of about 960 meters.

one does not make the challah of an am ha-aretz etc.. A person who is careful about impurity and purity (a 'chaver') who earns his living making doughs ('gabal') should not separate challah in purity for an am ha-aretz, lest it become impure. But if the am ha-aretz wishes to pay the chaver for the whole process of making the dough, they permitted the chaver to do so because this is his livelihood ('enough for his life'). And the chaver should do everything in his power so that the challah not become impure, by placing it in a vessel that does not receive impurity, and should warn the am ha-aretz to touch only the vessel and not the challah (see also Hilchot Terumot 12:9).
in dung vessels. Made of cattle dung and earth (Commentary to the Mishnah Kelim 10:1).

and they say to him: be careful lest you touch the challah, lest it return to tevel. Although the challah does not return to tevel because of his touching, they threaten him with this so that he not touch it and make the challah impure (Radbaz). Some explain that the challah indeed returns to tevel (for the Sages instituted that the chaver's separation of challah is conditional on the am ha-aretz not making it impure; Chatam Sofer, Gittin 62a).
sifting and sorting. Different stages of sifting flour.
with the wife of an am ha-aretz. For flour does not receive impurity before coming into contact with water.
kneading. Mixing flour with water.
working. With the hands, which is the act we call kneading (Commentary to the Mishnah Menachot 5:2).

they carry bread with him to the merchant. They help him carry the baked bread to the merchant who will buy it from him, since the transfer (causing impurity to the challah) has already been done (Commentary to the Mishnah Avodah Zarah 4:9).

just as all Israel in the Land were not suspected regarding great terumah. For the Sages decreed that one who buys from an am ha-aretz must separate tithes out of doubt because amei ha-aretz were not careful to separate tithes. But regarding great terumah they did not decree, since even amei ha-aretz were careful to separate it (see Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).

thus they were not suspected in Syria regarding challah. All the more so they were not suspected regarding challah in the Land of Israel, since, like terumah, challah carries a death penalty and can be separated easily because it has no minimum amount by Torah law (Radbaz). Some say that amei ha'aretz (the unlearned) were suspected regarding challah in the Land, and only in Syria, whose status is not Torah-based, was the rule relaxed (Yeshuot Malko, Hilchot Ma'aser 9:6).
must separate challah out of doubt. Because challah outside the Land of Israel is rabbinic (above 5:7), and bakers are suspected of neglecting it.
one who buys from a householder. One who buys from a private person who does not sell regularly.
one who slaughters. A slaughterer.
the foreleg, the jaws, and the stomach. See below, halachot 18-19.
and this shall be the priests' due. The verse continues: "from the people, from those who offer a sacrifice, whether ox or sheep: they shall give the priest the foreleg, the jaws, and the stomach."
in the time of the Temple. While the Temple stands.
consecrated animals. Animals consecrated to the Temple treasury or as offerings.

where a permanent blemish preceded their consecration etc.. That is, when he consecrated the animal it already had a permanent blemish that disqualifies it from being offered on the altar. Therefore the sanctity did not take effect on its body but on its value, and after it is redeemed it is entirely ordinary (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:11, Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9).

but if it preceded etc.. If at the time of consecration it had a passing blemish (one that disqualifies it only temporarily until it passes) or was unblemished, the sanctity of the body took effect, and even after a permanent blemish later arose and it was redeemed, it retains some sanctity (Hilchot Me'ilah, ibid.).

a doubtful firstborn. An animal about which there is doubt whether it is a firstborn. It is not given to the priest; rather, it must wait until a blemish arises, and the owners eat it (Hilchot Bechorot 5:3).
if it is a firstborn, all of it is the priest's. On the possibility that it is a firstborn, all of it must be given to the priest, including the gifts.

and if it is not a firstborn, its gifts are the priest's. On the possibility that it is not a firstborn, its gifts must be given to the priest, so that from either side the gifts belong to the priest (a definite firstborn is exempt from the gifts, since a consecrated animal is exempt from the gifts).

if there was doubt about two animals and the priest took one out of doubt. If one of them is certainly a firstborn but it is not known which, and the priest took one of them, the other is eaten by the owners when blemished, as the law of a doubtful firstborn.

they treated it as if the priest had acquired it and given it back to its owners in its blemished state. Although the priest did not take the second into his possession, the Sages regarded it as if the priest had received it as a firstborn and given it to the Israelite after a blemish arose, and so it is exempt from the gifts like a firstborn.
a doubtful tithe. A doubtful animal tithe. A definite tithe animal is offered as a sacrifice and the owners eat its meat; when it is doubtful it is eaten by the owners when blemished (see ibid. 6:4).

for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow. Since a tithe animal is exempt from the gifts, a priest who wants to take the gifts from the owner must bring proof that this animal is not a tithe animal.
when each animal belongs to a different person. If each animal belongs to a different owner.

if one person slaughters them all, he exempts the gifts of only one of them. Some understood from this wording of the Rambam that when one slaughterer slaughters the animals, even if each animal belongs to a different person, only one animal is exempt, since the priest can claim the gifts from the slaughterer (see further below, halacha 10, in the Rulings and Opinions) and the slaughterer cannot put him off with a claim of doubt. According to this, all the animals are exempt only when each belongs to a different person and is slaughtered by a different slaughterer (Shevet Sofer, Chullin 132a).
an animal. And not a wild animal or a bird.
a sheep or goat. A lamb or a goat.
and the koy. An animal that is in doubt whether it is a wild animal or a domestic animal (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 1:13, Hilchot Nezirut 2:10-11, Commentary on the Mishnah, Bikkurim 2:8).
even though it is in doubt, all the gifts are separated from it. By rabbinic enactment (see Rikuv and Radbaz).
a deer. A kosher wild animal.
the offspring is obligated in half the gifts. Because on its father's side it is exempt and on its mother's side it is obligated.
if it is a sheep, even part of a sheep. The Sages learned from the verse that the obligation of the gifts applies also to an animal that is not fully a domestic animal.

but a he-goat that mated with a doe, the offspring is exempt from the gifts. When the father is a domestic animal and the mother a wild animal, it is completely exempt, since the Sages were unsure whether one follows only the mother, so that it has the law of its mother in every respect, or one follows the father as well; and a priest who wants half the gifts must bring proof that one follows the father too (in the previous case, where its mother is a domestic animal, a priest who wants all the gifts must bring proof that one follows only the mother, so because of the doubt he is given only half the gifts; Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 132a).
one who buys an animal with the produce of the Sabbatical year. He bought an animal in exchange for Sabbatical-year produce or Sabbatical-year money.

is obligated in the gifts. Even though the sanctity of the Sabbatical year took effect on it (Hilchot Shemitah 6:7), since the gifts are meant for the priest to eat and giving them is not considered trade (compare Hilchot Bechorot 5:9).
the priests do not take from them. The priests do not take gifts from the Levites, because of the doubt.
and if the priest took them, he does not return them. Since the gifts are now in his possession, a Levite who wants to take them from him must bring proof that Levites are exempt.
they wait for him two or three Sabbaths. They wait to see whether he sells regularly.

they take the gifts from him and give them to other priests. Although the animal is his and by Torah law he is exempt from the gifts, the Sages enacted that he give them to others, so as not to accustom Jewish butchers to partner with him and be exempt (Tosafot, Chullin 132a).
Sabbaths. Weeks.
one who slaughters for a gentile or a priest. An animal belonging to a gentile or a priest.

and one who partners with a priest etc.. By Torah law an animal belonging to a priest and an Israelite is exempt from the gifts; however, the Sages were concerned about appearances and forbade the Israelite to take the gifts.
must mark his share so that he leaves the gifts in the priest's portion. He must mark his share and leave the gifts in the priest's portion.
specified. Defined, designated.
need not mark. And the Israelite may take the gifts, since everyone sees that the priest is a partner in the animal.
that he is a partner except for the gifts. That the Israelite is a partner with him in his animal, except for the gifts, which remain in the priest's possession.
if the priest reserved for himself a share in the gifts. The priest kept them for himself, and they were not included in the partnership at all.

if the priest said to him, on condition that the gifts are mine, then etc.. In this case the priest did not keep the gifts in his possession but included them in the partnership and stipulated that the Israelite give the gifts to him and not to another priest. Therefore the Israelite must give the gifts (because of appearances, as mentioned in the previous halacha), but he is not bound to keep the priest's condition, since by Torah law the owner may give to whichever priest he wishes, and a condition against Torah law has no validity.
a partner in the head. And not in the rest of the animal.
exempt from the jaw. And obligated in the foreleg and stomach as usual.
in the innards. The digestive system, or a term for all the internal organs.
of tevel. Untithed produce, which is forbidden to eat.

for the priestly gifts are distinct. The gifts are specific, defined parts even before they are separated (unlike tevel produce, where only at the time of separation does it become clear which produce is designated for the tithes).
who has no known claimant. Who does not belong to a particular priest.
even though he is not permitted. Since he assists the seller in robbing.
it is permitted for him to eat them. And he need not give them to a priest.

because priestly gifts can be taken by robbery. Therefore when the Israelite sold them, he is considered to have robbed the priests, and they pass into the possession of the person who bought them (and one cannot claim from the robber, since it is money with no claimants).
he gives them to the priest. For the gifts are not acquired by him, since the seller did not intend to rob them (unlike the previous halacha).

and he does not deduct from him from the price. He does not reduce the price by the value of the stomach; the seller can claim that the sum he collected does not include the stomach, which belongs to the priest.
he bought them from him by weight. And the butcher also charged for the weight of the gifts.

he need not worry that perhaps this one transgressed and robbed. The recipient need not worry that the sender robbed the gifts, for a person is presumed to be proper, and one should assume they came to him lawfully (for example, he bought them from the priest).
he assesses the gifts in money. He estimates their monetary value.
because of the priest's loss. Because they might spoil.
in each piece enough for a gift. An amount that is considered a proper quantity.
the right foreleg. The right front leg.

from the joint of the elbow to the palm of the hand. From the joint at the end of the bone of the upper arm attached to the body, downward to the hooves (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 4:6, 10:4).

for they are two limbs joined to one another. The foreleg includes two bones joined together (and it is possible to explain that these words refer to "the palm of the hand", explaining that the animal's hoof is meant, which is composed of two bones attached to each other).
from the joint of the jaw. From the place where the lower jaw connects with the skull.
up to the pikah of the windpipe. Up to the uppermost ring ("pikah") of the windpipe.
they do not scald. They do not put them in boiling water to remove the wool.
and they do not skin. The hide.
with the fat. Fat.
and they already practiced. Since the time of the Tannaim (Tosefta, Chullin 9:11).

a priest's wife eats the gifts... and furthermore, the husband etc.. The owner of the animal may give the gifts to a priest's daughter who is married to an Israelite, and even to her Israelite husband.
because they have no sanctity. They are only a monetary matter, unlike terumah, which is called holy and is not given to a priest's daughter married to an Israelite (see Hilchot Terumot 6:5).
a challalah. Whose father is a priest and whose mother is forbidden to a priest, or who herself had forbidden relations with a priest (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:1).
colleagues who give him the gifts. Regularly (in the language of the Gemara, "acquaintances of the priesthood").

even though they did not come into his hand etc.. Since he is accustomed to receive from them, it is considered as if he received the gifts from them even though they did not reach him, and he can acquire them on behalf of his fellow (see Hilchot Ma'aser 7:6).
they slaughter. Slaughter.
and his gatherer. One who works for him during the harvest and gathering seasons (Rashi, Eruvin 64a).
for anointing. In a manner of greatness and honor.
to give the priest the first of the shearing. When he shears his flock, he must give the priest a portion of the wool (and ideally he gives what he shears first, below, halacha 15).
in the time of the Temple. While the Temple stands.
like the first of the grain. Like terumah.
for the maintenance of the Temple. For the property of the Temple.
and sheared them. The Sages forbade shearing animals designated for the maintenance of the Temple (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:12); here the case is where he transgressed their words.
to redeem. A little of the wool, equal to the amount of the first of the shearing.
all sacred animals etc.. For an explanation of this halacha see above 9:2.
and in the robbery of a convert. If a convert was robbed and died without heirs, the robber pays the priests (Hilchot Gezelah 8:4-6).
and consecrated property that was devoted. If a person said of something of his property, "this is devoted", he gives it to the priests (Hilchot Arachin va'Charamin 6:1).
and an ancestral field. If a person consecrated his ancestral inheritance and another person redeemed it from the Temple treasury, in the Jubilee year it is given to the priests (ibid. 4:20).
in the inheritance. Land in the Land of Israel.
and in the spoils. Plunder taken at the time of the conquest of the cities of the Land of Israel (Hilchot Shemitah veYovel 13:10-11).
red or black etc.. The same applies to all shades of color (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 11:2).

he is exempt from the first of the shearing. Since he acquired all the wool by means of the change he made in it (Rashi, Chullin 135a; for acquisition of robbed property by change see Hilchot Gezelah 2:1, 2:12). However, it is forbidden to do this deliberately (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin, ibid.).
he whitened it. He washed it.
he must separate it after he has whitened it. For washing is not a change.
and did not shear it. He did not use a tool in the manner of shearing.
in a mixed breed. Whose mother is a sheep and whose father is a goat (Da'at Avot).
and in the koy. Even though it is in doubt whether it is a wild animal (see above 9:5, in the explanation).
and in a treifah. That was mauled by a predator and is expected to die (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:6-7), or that has an illness that makes it considered a treifah (see Hilchot Shechitah 5:2).
one who shears a dead animal is exempt. Since carcasses are not called a flock (see Kesef Mishneh and Da'at Avot in the explanation of the halacha).

is liable for its responsibility until he gives it to the priest. He must give the priest other wool from the fleece, for the fulfillment of the commandment is at the time of giving to the priest and not at the time of separating.
all my fleeces are first. That he did not leave any wool for himself.
the buyer. The purchaser.
who bought the flock for its shearing. He bought the right to shear the flock and take the wool.
sheared his fellow's flock. Before the shearing (and he did not buy the sheep themselves).
to separate from what remains for all. To give the priest from what he left for himself an amount that also exempts the buyer's portion.
a person does not sell priestly gifts. Who wants to fulfill the commandment.
and left. Kept for himself.
sixty sela. About 1,150 grams (according to the accepted view).
its commandment is at the beginning. To give from the wool he sheared at the beginning of the shearing.
all combine etc.. Since the commandment applies at the beginning of the shearing, all the sheep in his possession at that time combine, even if the shearing continues for several years.
and he may. He is permitted.
from the new for the old. From wool he sheared this year for wool he sheared last year.
and from one kind of fleece for another kind of fleece. For example, from white wool for black wool.
and left its fleece. For himself, that he did not sell the wool.
they do not combine. Even though he holds the wool of both, since the second was not his at the beginning of the shearing.

he gives him from the wool of the fleece while it is soiled etc.. Since the gift to the priest is of dirty wool that has not yet been washed ("tzo'i"), and some wool falls out in washing, the amount given must be adjusted accordingly.
like the gifts of an animal. Above 9:20.
for the law of both is the same. That it is permitted to give the first of the shearing to an Israelite married to a priest's daughter, but not to a challal, as stated there.
who is a firstborn to his mother. Even if he is not a firstborn to his father (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 8:1).
every first issue of the womb is Mine. Every offspring that first opens the womb belongs to Me. And through redemption he becomes his own.

for one who is obligated to redeem himself. And a daughter is not obligated in redemption, as it says "the firstborn of your sons you shall give Me" (Exodus 22:28), your sons and not your daughters (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 29a).
and none shall appear before Me empty-handed. This commandment refers to the pilgrimage, where the pilgrim must bring an offering (Hilchot Chagigah 1:1).
with five sela. Refined silver weighing 1,920 barleycorns (see Hilchot Eruvin 1:12), about 96 grams.
and those to be redeemed, from a month old shall you redeem. The verse continues: "by your valuation, five shekels of silver, by the shekel of the sanctuary."
with something worth money etc.. An object that has monetary value.
and not with slaves, because they are like land. Regarding Canaanite slaves the language of inheritance and holding is used (see Leviticus 25:46), like land (Hilchot Genevah 2:2).

and not with promissory notes, because their substance is not money. If another person owes the father a sum of money, the father cannot redeem his son by giving the debt document to the priest (even though the priest could collect money by means of the document), since the document itself has no monetary value and serves only as evidence (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 5:1).
he must give him. For he committed himself to it.
and his son is not redeemed. Even after he gave, as a decree lest people say that it is permitted to redeem with documents (Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 51b).
and the priest accepted it as five sela. The priest said that to him this object is worth five sela.
whether all at once. For example, he placed five sela before them and left (Rashi, Bechorot 51b).
or one after another. For example, he gave each priest a sela or half a sela.
if the priest wishes to return the redemption to him, he may return it. For the redemption money belongs to the priest and he may give it to whomever he wishes.
he may not give it to him intending that he return it. The father should not give with the thought in his mind that the priest will return it to him, for then the gift is not complete.

if he specified and gave it to him on condition to return it, his son is redeemed. In this case the father decided in his heart to give a complete gift for a limited time, and such a gift counts as a gift (Hilchot Zechiyah uMatanah 3:9).

if the Israelites' firstborn were exempted in the wilderness etc.. In the wilderness the firstborn were redeemed by taking the Levites in their place (see Numbers 3:40-51), so the sanctity of the Levite removed the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn; all the more so the sanctity of a Levite removes the sanctity of firstborn status when he is himself a firstborn (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 1:1).
for the matter does not depend on the father but on the mother. For the obligation of redemption applies only to a firstborn to his mother (as above, halacha 1).
a womb among Israel. And not the womb of a daughter of the tribe of Levi.
her mother was disqualified from the priesthood through relations with a gentile. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:3.
a priest who had a son who is a challal. A son from a woman forbidden to priests (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:3); the son is disqualified from the priesthood and obligated in redemption.
within thirty days. Before the time arrives at which the son becomes obligated in redemption (as below, halacha 17).

for the father has acquired his redemption. When the son reached thirty days, the obligation to redeem him fell on the father, and since the father is himself a priest he need not give five sela to another priest; thus the son is redeemed (and setting aside the redemption money is not essential, "for gifts fit to be separated are as if separated, even though they have not yet been separated", Hilchot Ma'aser 6:21).
a maidservant who was freed. A Canaanite maidservant, who from the time of her release becomes Israelite in every respect (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:12).
whose conception was not in sanctity. Whose mother conceived before she became Israelite.
and she has opened a womb among Israel. The opening of the woman's womb (the birth), which is the determining stage, took place after the woman converted, when she was already part of Israel.

the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow. The priest must bring proof that she converted before the birth, and if he has no proof, the redemption money remains with the firstborn's owner.
one who comes after miscarriages. A firstborn born after his mother's previous pregnancy ended in a miscarriage.

a miscarriage whose mother is impure by childbirth. A miscarriage whose delivery is considered a birth with regard to the impurity of a woman who has given birth (who is like a menstruant even though she did not see blood; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:1; the rest of that chapter details which miscarriage causes childbirth impurity).
like fish and locusts. Pieces of flesh that do not have a human facial form.
the fortieth day. Of her pregnancy.
a fetus that was cut up etc.. A fetus that was cut into limbs and came out of its mother that way.
