an eight-month child... and likewise a nine-month child who died etc.. These cases deal with a fetus that put out its head before its twin brother, then drew its head back, and its brother came out before it.
and once its forehead emerges etc.. The emergence of the forehead has the law of the emergence of the head.
one born by cesarean. A firstborn born by cesarean section.
and the one who comes after him in the normal way. The second son is born by an ordinary birth.
for he did not emerge from the womb. That he did not emerge through the opening of the womb, but through the wall of the womb.

and the second, because another preceded him. The second did indeed open the womb, but since he was not born first to his mother he is not considered a firstborn (see Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 47b).
once he completes thirty days. Therefore he is to be redeemed on the thirty-first day after birth.
and likewise if he became a treifah. Before he completed thirty days.
became a treifah. Was injured or fell ill in such a way that he will certainly die from it (Hilchot Rotze'ach 2:8).
he returns the redemption to him. Since the giving was in error.
from now. That the redemption take effect already now.
even though the coins no longer exist etc.. Since the priest received the coins for the purpose of redemption (see also Hilchot Ishut 7:10).
if the father died within thirty days, the son is presumed not redeemed. For a person usually does not pay his debt before its time (Hilchot Malveh veLoveh 11:6).
if the father died after thirty days, he is presumed redeemed. For presumably he redeemed the son on time and did not delay the commandment (Rambam LeAm; see Rashi, Bava Metzia 102b).
one whose wife had not given birth before and bore a male and a female. That in her first birth she bore twins.
for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow. And perhaps the firstborn died, and so he is entirely exempt from redemption.
whether after thirty days. And he had not yet redeemed.

for the property is already obligated. The father's property was bound for the redemption, even if he died before the obligation of redemption actually took effect (within thirty days). Even if the brothers have already divided the inheritance among themselves, they cannot put the priest off from one to another.
and one of them died within thirty days. And the law is that his redemption money returns to the father (above, halacha 17).
he did not specify this redemption for this son. He did not state that particular five sela were to redeem a particular son.
and each of them etc.. Since the money is already in their possession, and the burden of proof is on the father who wants to take it back.
the father died. And both children remained alive after thirty days.
five sela shall be given from the estate. As above, halacha 20.
if they gave to two priests, they cannot take it out of their hands. For each priest can claim that he received it for the living infant.
authorization. Power of attorney.

and he takes back five sela from the priest. For he can claim: if my baby died, return it to me, and if my fellow's died, return it to me on his behalf (and afterward they will divide it between them).
the fathers are exempt. For each can claim that the male who was born is not his son.
and the son must redeem himself. When he grows up, since he is certainly a firstborn.

a woman who had not yet given birth etc.. A woman who had not yet given birth, who was divorced from one husband and married another without waiting three months (as halacha requires; see Hilchot Gerushin 11:18), and bore a male seven months after the second marriage, so there is doubt whether he is the son of the first, in whose womb he stayed nine months, or of the last, in whose womb he stayed seven months.
two women bore two females etc.. Two wives of two men (as above, halacha 26), where each can claim that his wife bore the female first.

for he is exempt only through two doubts etc.. And above, halacha 25, regarding two wives of one man where one had not given birth and they bore two males and a female, the Rambam ruled that he is exempt even though there too there are two doubts, because in our halacha the man whose wife had not given birth must attribute the male to the woman who is not his in order to exempt himself, and the Rambam holds that one cannot make such a claim when there are two doubts (Rikuv and Kesef Mishneh).
the firstborn of a donkey. A male donkey that is the firstborn of its mother.
with a sheep. A lamb or a goat (below, halacha 8).
to break its neck. See below, halacha 7.
and the commandment of redemption takes precedence over the commandment of breaking the neck. For the main commandment is to redeem it, and that is the proper course.

as it is said, every first issue of the womb. The verse continues: "of all flesh that they offer to the Lord, whether of man or of beast, shall be yours," that is, Aaron's and his sons' (Rikuv and Kesef Mishneh; see Radbaz and the Shinui Nusach section of the Frankel edition, that perhaps the derivation is from the end of the verse quoted shortly below at the start of halacha 3).
is the donkey alone. As learned from the verse in the book of Exodus, "and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a sheep" (as cited above, halacha 1).

its proceeds are forbidden. It is forbidden to benefit from the money, because he received it in exchange for something forbidden to benefit from, at a time when he had the ability to redeem it (see Pitchei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah 321:1).

and the priests are suspected regarding this matter. They mistakenly think that once the donkey is in their possession it no longer needs redemption (Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 12b, according to Rashi there).
he set aside the redemption of a firstborn donkey etc.. He took a sheep and redeemed the firstborn donkey with it, but did not manage to give it to the priest.

he is not liable for its responsibility etc.. For the commandment is completed from the moment he redeems the donkey with the sheep (unlike redemption of a son, where the commandment is not complete until he gives the redemption money to the priest; Rosh, Bechorot 1:14), and from that moment the donkey becomes ordinary and the sheep belongs to the priest. Therefore he must give the priest the carcass of the sheep, and likewise if the donkey died after the sheep was set aside, he must give the sheep to the priest, and the donkey's carcass may be used.
and up to thirty days. That is the commandment ideally.
and this is only a delay of a commandment. For even after thirty days he does not transgress a prohibition, but only delays a commandment he is obligated in.
with a kufis. A cleaver used for cutting meat, for this is the manner of breaking the neck.
with an axe. An axe for chopping wood.
with a saw. A saw (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 17:2).
with a treifah. That was mauled by a predator and is expected to die (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:6-7), or that has an illness that makes it considered a treifah (see Hilchot Shechitah 5:2).
and not with a mixed breed. Even a sheep born of a male goat and a female sheep, both of whose parents are fit for redemption (Da'at Avot, based on the Rishonim).
and not with a koy. Which is in doubt whether it is a wild animal (see above 9:5, in the explanation).
one does not redeem with a lamb that resembles etc.. For example, both its parents are sheep and it looks like a goat.

with a ben pekuah. A fetus found alive in its mother's womb after she was slaughtered (and it is fit for redemption even though for the purpose of eating it is considered slaughtered; see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 5:14).
with disqualified consecrated animals. An animal that developed a blemish after it was consecrated as an offering, and was redeemed.
a lamb that he bought with Sabbatical-year money. That he bought with money that has the sanctity of the Sabbatical year, and the sanctity passed to the lamb (see Hilchot Shemitah 6:6-7).

one does not redeem with it a certain firstborn donkey. A definite firstborn donkey, because the sanctity of the Sabbatical year is meant for eating and not for trade, and he would be giving the priest a lamb and receiving in exchange a donkey that is not fit for eating (Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 12b and Rashi there).

one redeems with it a doubtful one. For example, two donkeys, a male and a female, were born to him and he does not know which came out first; he must set aside a lamb but does not give it to the priest (below, halacha 19). In this case it is permitted to redeem with a Sabbatical-year lamb, since it remains in his possession for eating.
he redeems it at its value. With money or something worth money, equal to the value of the donkey.
he may redeem it with a lamb worth a dinar. He may redeem it even with a lamb worth much less than the donkey, for a dinar is a quarter of a sela.
from consecrated property that is redeemed with money. From something consecrated to the Temple, which can be redeemed with money equal to its value.
zuzim. Dinars.
or with three zuzim. For an average person (as stated at the end of the halacha).

and a generous person etc.. A generous person redeems it with a sela, which is four zuzim, and a stingy person redeems it with half a sela, which is two zuzim (provided the donkey is not worth more than that).
and the donkey belongs to its owner. For the one who redeems does not acquire the donkey by the redemption, but only removes its prohibition.
and one exempt from a human firstborn. As stated above 11:9, that priests and Levites are exempt from redemption of a son.
one who buys the fetus of his donkey etc.. See also Hilchot Bechorot 4:1-3.
one who buys the fetus of a gentile's donkey. He buys the fetus while it is in its mother's womb, and did not buy its mother.

even though he is not permitted. For by selling it to a gentile he removes from it the law of a firstborn donkey, and ideally this should not be done (Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 2a, according to Tosafot's explanation there).

even if he had only one in a thousand of it. For example, he paid a small sum out of its value, but his share in the donkey is not defined, and therefore he is considered a partner in all of it. Unlike what is stated later in the halacha, where he has a specific limb (Kesef Mishneh).
anything that, if cut off, would make it blemished. As detailed in Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash chapter 7 and Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach chapter 2.
and likewise one who takes a donkey in partnership etc.. Who takes upon himself the care of the donkey in exchange for dividing the offspring between them.

he is liable etc.. For there is a doubt about a Torah prohibition, and the prohibition against benefiting must be removed from the donkey. But giving to the priest is a separate matter (see above, halacha 5) and is treated by the laws of monetary matters.
they inform him that he is not obligated. So that he should not say that Israelites treat sacred things lightly (Shach, Yoreh De'ah 321:13).
and it is permitted for shearing and work. An Israelite is permitted to benefit from its wool or to work with it, for it has no sanctity at all.
and if it has some etc.. A donkey that gave birth to something like a horse that has some signs of a donkey has the law of a donkey.
that had not yet given birth. That had not yet given birth.
two males and a female, he gives one lamb to the priest. For if one donkey bore two males, or a female and then a male, he has one male firstborn.

because there are many doubts here etc.. With regard to each donkey separately there is a doubt upon a doubt ("safek sefeika") whether a male firstborn was born to it (and here the doubts regarding the second donkey are detailed): first, one can doubt whether it bore a male at all ("perhaps one bore a male and the other two females"); and even if it bore a male, one can doubt whether it bore the male or the female first ("or perhaps this one bore a female, and the other a male followed by a female, or a female followed by a male"; according to Chazon Ish, Bechorot 17:1, and see Taz, Yoreh De'ah 321, subsection 11, who explained it differently).
because it is a doubt. Perhaps the male was born to the one that had previously given birth.

they are ordinary in every respect. For there is no sanctity in the lamb with which a firstborn donkey is redeemed, but it must be given to the priest, and when there is a doubt it remains in the owners' possession.
and they are tithed like the rest of the animals. For it is a commandment to separate one animal out of every ten kosher animals born to him (Hilchot Bechorot 6:1).
that came to him from his mother's father's house, a priest. That he inherited from his grandfather the priest.
he separates for them ten lambs. Since they were born in the house of his grandfather's grandfather, who is an Israelite, and became obligated in redemption.
and they are his. Since his priestly grandfather bequeathed to him his right, and just as his priestly grandfather could redeem and keep the lambs for himself, so he may do.
and they are subject to the tithe. As explained in the previous halacha.
